title: Auditing Radar Ghost Labels: Multipath Geometry, Detection, and Risk Control
content: Multipath “ghost” detections cause false tracks in automotive radar perception, and the Radar Ghost Dataset offers the only public manual multi-bounce labels known to us. Using its 111 stationary-ego sequences from 21 scenarios, grouped into eight site groups for leave-one-group-out evaluation, we examine how far these labels, and detectors trained on them, can be trusted. The findings concern moving ghosts of a moving pedestrian or cyclist seen by two 2D radars. Eight predictions were pre-registered, and they are kept apart from exploratory analyses throughout. A motion-aware audit finds that moving ignore-labelled detections exceed the null near model-predicted ghost positions by only about 1 % of the labelled ghost hits, against an apparent 20 % in a position-only audit that counts static returns; static ghosts and ghosts of other objects lie outside the audit. A forward multipath model built from lidar-reconstructed walls places 63–83 % of the labelled ghosts that have a candidate within 0.5 m of their mapped path construction on held-out groups. Rotating the wall set by one or two degrees collapses type-2 agreement but not type-1 agreement, and for image-path ghosts the Doppler predicted by the model correlates with the measured Doppler at 0.80, against 0.66 for the Doppler of the parent alone. A gradient-boosting detector on label-free features reaches a mean AUPRC of 0.66. Neural detectors given the same features and trained for twelve epochs match it, whereas a point network without wall and density features reaches 0.48. In a five-seed ablation, lidar-wall geometry adds 0.10 AUPRC (not significant after correction), Doppler dominates, and removing position information altogether does not lower AUPRC (0.68). Learn-then-Test kept the loss of real pedestrians and cyclists below 0.05 in all eight held-out folds while removing 45 % of ghost detections, an empirical and conservative result under group shift. At scenario level only targets above about 0.12 would be certifiable, although calibrating with scenarios as the units (with non-nested scores) held the loss below target in all folds from a target of 0.15; group-conditional control is infeasible. A tracker fed by conformal risk control cut main-object ghost tracks from 11.7 to 3.3 per minute at a cost of 3.5 points of real-track recall. Mining of missed ghosts and two-radar cues did not help, and these negative results are reported with diagnostics.
